Brain tumour: Progressive focal signs + contrast‑enhancing mass on MRI + histology (if biopsied) — WHO tumour grade I‑IV; functional status by Karnofsky Performance Scale
| Brain tumour (acute presentation) | Progressive symptoms, seizures, constitutional signs | Imaging shows mass lesion with contrast enhancement; slower onset. |
Look‑alike conditions: hypoglycaemia, seizure with post‑ictal deficit, brain tumour, meningitis, conversion disorder.
Structural: Brain tumour, abscess, hydrocephalus — HIV (primary CNS lymphoma), TB (tuberculoma), sickle cell disease (stroke)
Space‑occupying lesions: Large tuberculoma, cerebral abscess (bacterial, fungal, malaria‑related), primary brain tumour, metastatic disease
| Brain tumour (e.g., astrocytoma) | Progressive symptoms, seizures, focal deficits | MRI shows enhancing mass, often slower onset |

Too little vitamin A can lead to night blindness, and too much can make you think you have a (pseudo)tumor — hypervitaminosis A can raise intracranial pressure, mimicking a brain tumour (pseudotumor cerebri).

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with multiple early-onset cancers and a family history of sarcomas and brain tumours. Genetic testing confirms Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Which gene harbours a germline mutation in this condition?
qs.e: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is characterised by a germline mutation in the TP53 tumour suppressor gene, leading to multiple early-onset cancers. BRCA1 mutations are associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Brain tumours are abnormal growths in the central nervous system that can be benign or malignant. They present with focal neurological deficits, headaches, or seizures, and are diagnosed by imaging and histology. Management combines surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy tailored to tumour type.

sections.p: A brain tumour is a mass of proliferating neural or glial cells within the skull. Diagnosis starts with clinical suspicion, confirmed by MRI with contrast, and final histology after biopsy or resection.
b: MRI is first‑line imaging; CT if MRI unavailable. Histology distinguishes benign from malignant and guides therapy.

sections.p: Staging uses the WHO grading system (I–IV) for gliomas and the TNM system for metastatic lesions. Grade reflects proliferation, necrosis, and vascularity.
b: Grade I: low‑grade, slow growth; Grade IV: highly aggressive, poor prognosis.

sections.p: Primary causes are genetic mutations (e.g., IDH, EGFR), environmental exposures, and viral infections. In low‑resource settings, infections such as neuro‑tuberculosis and HIV‑associated lymphoma are common.
Symptoms depend on location: seizures, focal weakness, visual changes, personality shifts, or increased intracranial pressure causing headache and vomiting.
b: Sudden onset focal deficit suggests high‑grade tumour.

sections.p: Imaging and histology are core. When resources are limited, CT can detect mass effect, and cytology from CSF may aid diagnosis.
b: If MRI is unavailable, use CT and consider referral for advanced imaging.

t.b: Detects tumour location, size, and enhancement pattern; indicates blood‑brain barrier disruption.
Shows mass effect and calcification; useful when MRI unavailable.
Provides histological grade and molecular markers for targeted therapy.
Identifies leptomeningeal spread or infectious causes when tumour is not visible.

sections.p: Rapid neurological decline, seizures, vomiting, papilledema, or new focal deficits warrant urgent evaluation. Complications include hydrocephalus, cerebral oedema, and malignant transformation.
Treatment is multimodal: maximal safe resection, followed by radiotherapy and chemotherapy based on tumour type. Supportive care includes steroids for oedema and antiepileptics.
b: Temozolomide for glioblastoma; alkylating agents for other high‑grade tumours.

sections.p: Regular MRI surveillance detects recurrence. Prevention focuses on minimizing radiation exposure and managing infections that can lead to secondary tumours.
Stroke, subdural haematoma, and meningitis can mimic tumour symptoms.
b: Stroke: sudden onset, often vascular territory.

sections.p: Normal CSF opening pressure can occur in early tumours; CT may miss small enhancing lesions.
b: CT may appear normal in low‑grade tumours.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden neurological deficit, new seizures, severe headache with vomiting, visual changes, or any sign of raised intracranial pressure.

faq.q: Can a brain tumour be cured?
faq.a: Some low‑grade tumours can be cured with surgery alone; high‑grade tumours are managed but rarely cured.

faq.q: Do all brain tumours need surgery?
faq.a: Only if they are accessible and causing symptoms; some are treated with radiotherapy or chemotherapy alone.

faq.q: What is the role of steroids?
faq.a: They reduce cerebral oedema and improve symptoms but do not treat the tumour itself.
